extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and advanced undergraduates in functional analysis / PDEs
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts definitions, theorems and operative criteria from chapters on compact self-adjoint operators, Fredholm and Hilbert–Schmidt operators, the Krein–Rutman theorem, and the Hille–Yosida theory of maximal monotone operators and associated evolution problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fredholm operator (definition and index)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ∈ L(E, F) is a Fredholm operator if (i) N(A) is finite-dimensional and (ii) R(A) is closed and has finite codimension. The index is ind A = dim N(A) — codim R(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A = I − T with T ∈ K(E) is Fredholm of index zero (follows from Theorem 6.6). Note: if N(A) finite-dimensional and R(A) has finite codimension then R(A) is closed (see Exercise 2.27).

rubrics_metrics.name: Main properties of Fredholm operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Properties listed for the class (Φ)(E,F) of Fredholm operators: (a) Φ(E,F) is open in L(E,F) and ind A is continuous (constant on connected components); (b) every A ∈ Φ(E,F) is invertible modulo finite-rank operators (existence of B with A◦B − I_F and B◦A − I_E finite-rank) and conversely such approximate inverses imply A ∈ Φ(E,F); (c) stability under compact perturbations: if A ∈ Φ(E,F) and T ∈ K(E,F) then A+T ∈ Φ(E,F) and ind(A+T)=ind(A); (d) composition: if A ∈ Φ(E,F), B ∈ Φ(F,G) then B◦A ∈ Φ(E,G) and ind(B◦A)=ind A + ind B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References and further development: Kato, Schechter, Lang, Taylor–Lay, Lax, Hörmander. See Problem 38 in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert–Schmidt operator (definition and kernel characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: T ∈ L(H) (H separable Hilbert) is Hilbert–Schmidt if there exists a Hilbert basis (e_n) with ||T||_{HS}^2 = Σ |T e_n|^2 < ∞. This definition is independent of basis and defines a norm. Every Hilbert–Schmidt operator is compact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 6.12: On H = L^2(Ω) any K(x,y) ∈ L^2(Ω×Ω) defines a Hilbert–Schmidt operator (Ku)(x)=∫ K(x,y)u(y) dy, and conversely every HS operator on L^2(Ω) is of this form for a unique K∈L^2(Ω×Ω). See references and Problem 40.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity of eigenvalues (ascent/geometric/algebraic multiplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: For T ∈ K(E) and λ ∈ σ(T)\{0}, the sequence dim N((T−λI)^k) increases strictly up to some finite p (the ascent) and then stabilizes. Geometric multiplicity = dim N(T−λI); algebraic multiplicity = dim N((T−λI)^p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a Hilbert space for self-adjoint T the geometric and algebraic multiplicities coincide. See cited references and Problem 36.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectral analysis and spectral family (functional calculus)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a (possibly unbounded) self-adjoint operator T on a Hilbert space there is a spectral family extending the spectral decomposition of compact self-adjoint operators; this yields a functional calculus allowing the definition of f(T) for continuous f, and extends to normal operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectral analysis is extensive; see Rudin, Kreyszig, Friedman, Yosida for elementary accounts and Reed–Simon, Kato, Dunford–Schwartz, Akhiezer–Glazman, Conway, Lax, Schechter for advanced treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Min–max principle (Courant–Fischer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The min–max formulas of Courant–Fischer provide a practical method to compute eigenvalues of (self-adjoint) operators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used widely; see Courant–Hilbert, Lax, Weinberger (monograph) and Problem 37 for further developments and applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Krein–Rutman theorem (positive eigenvector in cones)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let E be a Banach space and P a closed convex cone with vertex 0, Int P ≠ ∅, P ≠ E. If T ∈ K(E) satisfies T(P\{0}) ⊂ Int P, then there exist x0 ∈ Int P and λ0>0 with T x0 = λ0 x0; λ0 is the unique eigenvalue with eigenvector in P (any such eigenvector is a positive scalar multiple of x0), λ0 = max{|λ|; λ ∈ σ(T)}, and its multiplicity (geometric and algebraic) equals one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof presented in Problem 41 (Rabinowitz). Variants in Schaefer, Nussbaum, Bonsall, Toland. Useful for spectral properties of second-order elliptic operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectral decomposition for compact self-adjoint operators
rubrics_metrics.description: For T compact self-adjoint on H, H decomposes as an orthogonal direct sum H = ⊕_{n≥0} E_n where each E_n is an eigenspace (E_0 = ker T), one can choose Hilbert bases in each E_n and their union is a Hilbert basis of H of eigenvectors. Any u ∈ H decomposes u = Σ_{n=0}^∞ u_n with u_n ∈ E_n, and T u = Σ_{n=1}^∞ λ_n u_n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite-rank truncations T_k = Σ_{n=1}^k λ_n P_{E_n} satisfy ||T_k − T|| ≤ sup_{n≥k+1} |λ_n| → 0. Remark: every compact operator (not necessarily self-adjoint) is the limit of finite-rank operators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of monotone and maximal monotone operators
rubrics_metrics.description: An (unbounded) linear operator A: D(A)⊂H→H is monotone if (A v, v) ≥ 0 ∀v∈D(A). It is maximal monotone if additionally R(I + A) = H, i.e., ∀f ∈ H ∃u ∈ D(A) with u + A u = f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative terminology: some authors say A is accretive or −A dissipative. Maximal monotonicity is the central hypothesis for Hille–Yosida evolution theory presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic properties of a maximal monotone operator (Proposition 7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is maximal monotone then: (a) D(A) is dense in H; (b) A is closed; (c) for every λ>0, I + λA is bijective D(A)→H, (I + λA)^{-1} is bounded with ||(I + λA)^{-1}||_{L(H)} ≤ 1; moreover surjectivity for some λ_0 implies surjectivity for all smaller factors by contraction mapping argument (conclusion: I + λA surjective for all λ>0 after iteration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses monotonicity and contraction mapping; (I + A)^{-1} is a bounded linear operator with norm ≤1, uniqueness of solutions for u + Au = f, and closedness of A follows from stability under limits via (I + A)^{-1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolvent J_λ and Yosida approximation A_λ (definitions and properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: For maximal monotone A and λ>0 define J_λ = (I + λA)^{-1} (the resolvent) and A_λ = (1/λ)(I − J_λ) (the Yosida approximation). The text lists key properties: (a1) A_λ v = A(J_λ v) for all v∈H, λ>0; (a2) A_λ v = J_λ(Av) for v∈D(A); (b) |A_λ v| ≤ |A v| for v∈D(A); (c) J_λ v → v as λ→0 for all v∈H; (d) A_λ v → A v for v∈D(A); (e) (A_λ v, v) ≥ λ |A_λ v|^2; (f) |A_λ v| ≤ (1/λ)|v| for all v∈H, λ>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: A_λ are bounded operators approximating the (possibly unbounded) A; usually ||A_λ|| blows up as λ→0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy–Lipschitz (Picard) existence and uniqueness for ODEs in Banach spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: If F: E→E is Lipschitz with constant L (||F u − F v|| ≤ L||u − v||) then for any u_0 ∈ E there exists a unique solution u ∈ C^1([0,∞); E) of du/dt = F(u(t)), u(0)=u_0. The proof uses contraction mapping in an exponentially weighted sup-norm space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem is classical and used in the text to solve approximate (bounded) problems before passing to limits in unbounded-operator evolution problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hille–Yosida theorem for maximal monotone operators (existence/uniqueness of evolution)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is maximal monotone then for any u_0 ∈ D(A) there exists a unique u ∈ C^1([0,∞); H) ∩ C([0,∞); D(A)) solving du/dt + A u = 0, u(0)=u_0. Moreover |u(t)| ≤ |u_0| and |du/dt(t)| = |A u(t)| ≤ |A u_0| for all t≥0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy: approximate A by bounded A_λ, solve ODEs via Cauchy–Lipschitz, derive λ-independent estimates, pass to limit λ→0. Consequence: defines contraction semigroup S_A(t) on H with properties: contraction, semigroup law, strong continuity at 0. Conversely continuous contraction semigroups correspond uniquely to maximal monotone generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 7.1: monotonicity of norms for solutions of dw/dt + A_λ w = 0
rubrics_metrics.description: If w ∈ C^1([0,∞); H) satisfies dw/dt + A_λ w = 0 then the functions t ↦ |w(t)| and t ↦ |dw/dt(t)| = |A_λ w(t)| are nonincreasing on [0,∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses (A_λ w, w) ≥ 0 (from Proposition 7.2(e)) and differentiates norms; applied inductively to higher derivatives to show monotonicity for all orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 7.2: density of D(A^2) in D(A) (graph norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: For maximal monotone A, D(A^2) is dense in D(A) with respect to the graph norm: given u_0∈D(A) and ε>0 there exists u_0^ε ∈ D(A^2) with ||u_0^ε − u_0|| < ε and ||A u_0^ε − A u_0|| < ε.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: take u_0^ε = J_λ u_0 for suitably small λ>0; then u_0^ε ∈ D(A^2) and J_λ approximates identity on D(A) as λ→0 (Proposition 7.2). This lemma is used to approximate general initial data by smoother ones for the existence proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity theorem (Theorem 7.5) for higher domains D(A^k)
rubrics_metrics.description: If u_0 ∈ D(A^k) for some integer k ≥ 2, then the solution u of du/dt + A u = 0 satisfies u ∈ C^{k−j}([0,∞); D(A^j)) for every j = 0,1,...,k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by induction: treat A as a maximal monotone operator on H_1 = D(A) with graph norm, observe A_1 (restriction) is maximal monotone on H_1, then apply Theorem 7.4 iteratively to gain regularity in time and space derivatives. Definition: D(A^k) recursively defined and endowed with equivalent Hilbert norms combining norms of A^j u.
